A Study of Scale and Belonging

A playable research prototype about getting lost in Rome, told through three body scales: ant, human and giant.

Games
VR
Spatial cognition
HCI
Design fiction
Social good

Origin

One evening in Rome my phone died. I walked home by memory and a sense of direction.

Rome's streets run long and straight, so I only needed to know which way home was. It felt like solving a maze from above.

On the way I took a detour I had never walked, and found a huge, open park hidden behind the rows of houses I pass every day.

I felt how small a person is. If I were taller than the buildings, could I see the horizon from inside a dense block?

Concept

When we feel lost, on a street or in life, we wish for a god's-eye view before choosing a way. The game grants it in small doses: at each street corner, 5 seconds as a giant. Home stands for belonging; the point is not the fastest route but what you meet on the way.

ScaleEye heightWhat you seeHow it feels
Ant1.2 cmGrey-black ground to the horizon. A kerb is a cliff, a cola can a wall.Oppressive, like outer space
Human1.7 mBusy streets, the same houses and shops on every side.Boxed in, bored, lost
Giant70 mOver the roofs: the hidden park, the hills beyond the city.Relief, openness, awe

Ant and giant both see "endless space", but not the same kind: the ant's is empty and heavy, the giant's is varied and beautiful.

Process &
Development

The city was first planned as a grid: 12 x 12 blocks of 40 m, streets of 10 m, like the long straight streets of Rome.

A hidden park fills the north-east corner, walled in by a ring of taller buildings, so it cannot be seen from street level. Start and home sit on opposite sides of it.

The plan was turned into a 3D massing with heights between 14 and 24 m, and 26 to 32 m for the ring around the park.

It was then built in three.js: ochre and terracotta facades, red tile roofs, cobbles, shops, Vespas, umbrella pines.

Narrative &
Storyboard

The game's nine beats follow Freytag's pyramid and the Hero's journey, as framed in Ellen Lupton's Design Is Storytelling. Each beat unlocks a mechanic: the body scale is the story.

01 · EXPOSITION

Ordinary world

“7 pm. A long day out. Phone dies.”

Mechanic Start at human scale. Only 2 HUMAN is active.

02 · EXPOSITION

Call to adventure

“Home is north-east. No map.”

Mechanic A goal without a route: walk by direction.

03 · RISING ACTION

Refusal

“Every street looks the same.”

Mechanic The grid repeats. Tall walls hide landmarks.

04 · RISING ACTION

Meeting the mentor

“A pigeon: "Wrong size." Press 1.”

Mechanic Reaching the fountain unlocks ANT.

05 · RISING ACTION

Crossing the threshold

“Small now. A kerb is a cliff.”

Mechanic Eyes at 1.2 cm. Kerbs block the way.

06 · CLIMAX

The ordeal

“Now the opposite. Press 3.”

Mechanic After 8 s as an ant, GIANT unlocks.

07 · CLIMAX

Reward

“A park you have never seen.”

Mechanic From 70 m the park is "found" from above.

08 · FALLING ACTION

The road back

“Come down. Walk the new way.”

Mechanic Back to HUMAN; the route crosses the park.

09 · DENOUEMENT

Return with the elixir

“Home. A different map in your head.”

Mechanic Finish: your path is drawn as a map.

VR Setup & Experience

The city is built in three.js, which supports WebXR: the same scene can open in a headset's browser, such as a Meta Quest 3, with no app to install.

In VR the player walks with the thumbstick and changes scale with a button. Instead of lifting the camera 70 m, the whole world shrinks or grows around the body, so head movement stays true to life. A short fade replaces the zoom to avoid motion sickness.

Concept visualisation. The current prototype runs on desktop; the WebXR build is the next step.

The final experience is a walk without a map: players do not follow a route, they read the city through the size of their own body.

The most valuable thing this project taught me is that perspective is not only where you look from. It is how big you are when you look.

Research

Does briefly changing body scale in a virtual city change how people understand the space, and how they feel about being lost in it? A pilot with three conditions: human only, human + giant at corners, and all scales.

RQ1

Spatial knowledge

Do giant views build a better mental map? Sketch maps and pointing to home.

RQ2

Discovery

Does a change of scale reveal places people would miss? Places found, path shape.

RQ3

Emotion

Does scale change the feeling of being lost? Awe scale and self-ratings.

RQ4

Reflection

Does it change how people think about feeling lost in life? Interviews.
